Chapter 2. Basic Topology

Countability and Uncountability

Thm. 2.12.

Countable union of countable sets is countable.

Proof

Enumerate the elements diagonally, e.g. x11,x12,x13,…x_{11},x_{12},x_{13},\ldotsx11​,x12​,x13​,…, x21,x22,x23,…x_{21},x_{22},x_{23},\ldotsx21​,x22​,x23​,…, …

Thm. 2.13.

Set of finite tuples whose elements are in a countable set is countable: (a1,…,an)(a_1,\ldots,a_n)(a1​,…,an​).

Proof

Induction. Let BnB_nBn​ be the set of n-tuples. The (n+1)(n+1)(n+1)-tuples are obtained from Bn×B1B_n\times B_1Bn​×B1​; apply Thm. 2.12.

Cor.

The set of all rational numbers is countable.

Thm. 2.14.

Let AAA be the set of all sequences whose elements are 0 or 1. Then AAA is uncountable.

Proof

Let E={s1,s2,…}E=\{s_1,s_2,\ldots\}E={s1​,s2​,…} be a countable subset of AAA. Construct sss such that its n-th digit differs from the n-th digit of sns_nsn​. Then s∉Es\notin Es∈/E; every countable subset of AAA is proper.

Convexity, Limit Points, and Open Sets

Def. (Convex).

E⊂RkE\subset\mathbb{R}^kE⊂Rk is convex if, for x,y∈Ex,y\in Ex,y∈E and 0≤λ≤10\le\lambda\le10≤λ≤1,

λx+(1−λ)y∈E.\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in E.λx+(1−λ)y∈E.

Definitions.

  • Limit point: ppp is a limit point of EEE if Nr∗(p)∩E≠∅N_r^*(p)\cap E\ne\varnothingNr∗​(p)∩E=∅ for every r>0r>0r>0.

  • Closed: every limit point of EEE belongs to EEE.

  • Interior point: some neighborhood Nr(p)N_r(p)Nr​(p) is contained in EEE.

  • Open: every point is an interior point.

  • Perfect: closed, and every point is a limit point.

  • Dense: every point is a limit point or a point of EEE (with respect to the ambient space).

Thm. 2.20.

A neighborhood of a limit point contains infinitely many points of the set.

Proof

If it contained only finitely many other points qmq_mqm​, choose a smaller radius using min⁡d(p,qm)\min d(p,q_m)mind(p,qm​), a contradiction.

Ex. Z\mathbb{Z}Z is closed, not open.

Sets A,BA,BA,B are separated if A∩B‾=∅A\cap\overline B=\varnothingA∩B=∅ and A‾∩B=∅\overline A\cap B=\varnothingA∩B=∅.

EEE is connected if it cannot be written as a union of two nonempty separated sets.
